rationale: A wins because it spotted the live business-model story B threw in the bin: "Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost, including Airtable" is uncomfortable, grounded in the unfinished-pricing fact, and useful to a SaaS economics reporter. B is disciplined, but calling "What Airtable will charge for agents and what that says about AI pricing" a "no_why_now_but_required" miss is backwards; the why-now is that Airtable is shipping agents before pricing is finalized. A also gives the founder sharper triage: pitch the repositioning now, park governance until reliability proof exists, and decide whether to invite the valuation fight.
gaps_in_A: "bets the company on agents" overstates the supplied facts. Repositioning is real; a company-level all-in wager is not stated.
"established category leader" and the Notion/Smartsheet/Monday comparison are plausible market context, but they are not in the fact block.
"Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost" reaches past the evidence. Airtable has not finalized pricing; the whole category has not been proven unsettled.
gaps_in_B: "What Airtable will charge for agents and what that says about AI pricing" being refused as "no_why_now_but_required" is the big miss. Unfinalized pricing at launch is a story, not a reason to kill it.
No kept pricing angle means B misses the buyer-economics protagonist entirely: what enterprise customers will pay when software starts doing actions instead of just storing records.
"software companies marked down from their peak try to earn their way back" adds market color not supplied by the update. Useful hypothesis, not a fact.
"once you pick one angle and have an on-record executive" is too generic as a next step. The founder needs sequencing, not a shrug in a blazer.
